$comment: The one place colour is decided. `pnpm run theme` turns this into
src/themeTokens.generated.ts, which the app reads at startup and on
every theme switch — both for the CSS custom properties and for the
colours handed to the wasm renderer.
Everything is authored in OKLCH, where lightness and chroma mean the
same thing at every hue. That is what makes a set of colours read as
one family instead of a pile: the palette this replaced ran from
L 0.56 to L 0.94 and from C 0.11 to C 0.30, with three greens and two
purples nobody had compared.
The character is poster paint — Bauhaus blocks, kindergarten
primaries. Sampling those references in OKLCH says what that means
in numbers, and it is not a flat ramp:
warm hues carry high chroma      red C 0.20-0.24, orange C 0.19
yellow is light, not just yellow L 0.86 at C 0.17
cool hues sit lower in chroma    blue C 0.10-0.15, green C 0.10
lightness follows the hue        yellow 0.86, red 0.63, blue 0.55
So each hue gets its own lightness and chroma rather than a shared
pair. A flat ramp is what made the last attempt look washed out: it
held every hue to the chroma only blue and green wanted.
The one place we leave the references: cool hues are lifted for a
dark background. A blue at L 0.55 is a poster colour on white and a
smudge on near-black.
Against the dark editor the poster values read as lit from inside,
so every hue is pulled down together: chroma to 0.9 of the
reference, lightness by 0.01 (0.02 for yellow, the brightest). One
factor for all eight keeps the family intact, which is the reason
for authoring in OKLCH in the first place. 0.8 was a step too far:
the palette went chalky.
$comment_steps: Three steps per hue, as offsets from the hue's own pair. `dim` is
for light backgrounds and quiet states, `bright` for the few things
that have to jump off a dark one. Chroma eases off at both ends:
sRGB has less of it to give away from mid lightness, and forcing it
there is what produces a colour that looks lit from inside.
$comment_neutral: Grey, and actually grey: chroma 0. An earlier version carried a
trace of blue on the theory that it would sit better beside the
hues. On a near-black panel it reads as a colour, which is the one
thing a neutral must not do.
The steps are lightness in percent, chosen so the ramp lands on the
greys the editor was drawn around — 15 is #0c0c0c, 37 is #404040,
65 is #909090. They mean the same in every theme: a light theme
takes its surfaces from the other end, it does not renumber them.

light.name: Light
light.$comment: Surfaces come from the other end of the same ramp; the hues drop to their dim step so they hold up on white.

gray.name: Gray
gray.$comment: Mid grey with dark ink, after runebender.org: square corners, and rules drawn in the text colour rather than a lighter tint, so the borders draw the layout instead of tints doing it. It takes the colour of the site's rules and not their weight: 2px reads as structure on a web page with room around it, and as heavy at editor density. The role hues stay coloured, since a point type you cannot tell apart is a usability cost the website never has to pay.

$comment_marks: How a glyph mark is drawn, not just which colour it is. On a near
black or near white canvas a hue can simply be lighter or darker
than the ground, so tinting the cell's border is enough. On a mid
grey there is nowhere to go: a colour saturated enough to read as a
hue sits at mid lightness too, and mid on mid is invisible. Gray's
yellow against its panel measured 1.00 contrast, which is not dim,
So the treatment is a theme's decision:
style   border  tint the cell's rule, leave the fill alone
fill    fill the cell with the hue and key it with a rule
outline the keyline colour, for style fill
ink     the label colour drawn on top of a filled mark
Fill works on any ground because the hue stops competing with the
background and becomes it, and the dark keyline separates the cell
regardless of what the two luminances are doing.
$comment_ufoMarkColors: What `public.markColor` gets in the UFO, frozen. These came from
the original hue values and must not follow later tuning of the
palette: they are file contents, shared with runebender-web, and a
font full of marked glyphs must not churn because a colour was
made quieter on screen. `mark_label_for_glyph` snaps a stored
colour to the nearest label by hue, so a mark written years ago
still resolves after the display palette moves.
$comment_geometry: Shape, not colour. A theme decides its corner radii and its rule
weights the same way it decides its greys, because those carry as
much of a UI's character as hue does: the same palette at radius 0
with a 2px rule reads as a drawing tool, and at radius 6 with a
The tokens are named for what they are used on, not for their size,
so a theme that disagrees about the sizes still knows what each one
radius          the default corner, on small chrome
radiusControl   pressable tiles: toolbar tiles, tabs, toggles
stroke          the ordinary rule, on panels and chrome
strokeEmphasis  rings that mark a thing selected or grabbable
strokeEmphasis is its own token rather than stroke doubled. Doubling
works from a 1px base and breaks from a 2px one: a 4px ring on an
Values are in px. A theme names only what it changes; anything it
leaves out falls back to `default` below.
